item.title: Antiquity
item.description:
Source: TW

Even a novice with some itihAsa-purAna background will note that the bhAgavata is linguistically rather unique. If you have spent some time with the mahAbhArata, harivaMsha, and the viShNupurANa, this distinctness will be even more apparent. It will become clear that while it belongs to their tradition in the broad sense, it has been crafted in a very different way – it is not a foundationally sauta text.+++(5)+++

Hence, E. Bryant has a point that it is an unparalleled project. It is also obvious to anyone who has studied the shruti that the author(s) were intimately acquainted with not just the vedic text but also shrauta praxis. There were such brAhmaNa-s with a vaiShNava bent or affiliation in South India. So it is tempting to claim it was composed de novo in South India due to the praise of southern devotees.

item.title: Yuga & avatAra
item.description:
Source: TW

The bhAgavata, as a later text, certainly shows influences of the ancient tradition from the early pa~ncharAtra expounded in the mahAbhArata. For example, the veda-restoring haMsa comes in both in the kR^ita. A complete treatment of the vibhava-s of the bhAgavata will take a lot of effort; hence, I’ll just restrict myself to some snippets. The treta is said to feature the following vibhava-s:

viShNur yaj~naH pR^ishni-garbhaH
sarvadeva urukramaH | vR^iShAkapir jayantash cha
urugAya itIryate ||
